title: Bats are NOT blind. The 'blind as a bat' myth is wrong.
sources: Bat Conservation International, USGS, Current Biology
answer: They are not. All bats have working eyes and can see. Vision varies by species, and some bats see better than people in the dark. Many bats use echolocation and sight together.
source_links: Bat Conservation International: Blind as a Bat? No Such Thing
Current Biology: Bats: Vision or echolocation, why not both?

title: Sugar does NOT make kids hyper
answer: It does not. A 1995 JAMA meta-analysis pooled 23 blinded, placebo-controlled studies and found that sugar does not affect children's behaviour or thinking. Parents who expect a sugar rush tend to see one, which is expectation. The authors note a small effect, or an effect in some subsets of children, can't be ruled out.
source_links: Wolraich, Wilson and White, JAMA 1995: The Effect of Sugar on Behavior or Cognition in Children (meta-analysis)

title: Cracking your knuckles does NOT cause arthritis
myth: Cracking your knuckles gives you arthritis.
answer: It probably doesn't. Studies comparing habitual knuckle-crackers with non-crackers found no higher rate of hand arthritis. The pop is bubbles bursting in the joint fluid. There is a catch: chronic cracking may reduce grip strength, and a couple of injuries have been reported.
source_links: Harvard Health: Does cracking knuckles cause arthritis?

title: Goldfish remember for months. Not 3 seconds.
description: The Professor gets it wrong. Fact Check has the real answer.
answer: They don't. Goldfish can learn and remember things for months. In experiments they learn feeding times, which side of the tank food arrives on, and which coloured paddle to push, and they still remember it long after the training.

title: Shaving doesn't thicken hair. The razor tip tricks your eyes.
description: The Professor gets it wrong. Fact Check has the real answer.
myth: Shaving makes your hair grow back thicker.
answer: It doesn't. Shaving cuts each hair straight across at its widest point, so the regrowing stubble has a blunt tip instead of a fine tapered one. That makes it feel coarser and look darker. The hair itself, and the follicle under the skin, are unchanged.

title: You DON'T use just 10% of your brain
description: The Professor gets it wrong. Fact Check has the real answer. Source: Scientific American.
myth: You only use 10% of your brain.
answer: You use all of it. Brain scans show activity across the whole brain over a day, and even during sleep many regions stay busy. Damage to almost any part of the brain has effects, which would not be true if 90% sat idle.
sources: Scientific American (neurologists Barry Gordon, Johns Hopkins, and John Henley, Mayo Clinic)

title: Lightning DOES strike twice
description: The Professor insists lightning never strikes the same place twice. Fact Check shows it does, all the time.
myth: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
answer: It does, and often. Tall, pointed and isolated objects get hit again and again, sometimes more than once in a single storm. Lightning does not avoid places it has already hit.
sources: US National Weather Service, Live Science (lightning expert Martin Uman, University of Florida)

title: Your stomach can dissolve a razor blade
description: The Professor is horrified by what stomach acid can do. Fact Check explains the catch.
myth: Your stomach acid can dissolve a razor blade.
answer: In a lab dish, simulated stomach acid can corrode metal objects over time. That is the catch: a swallowed blade does not sit there long enough to dissolve, and it can cut you on the way through. This is a fun fact, not a challenge.
sources: Li et al., "In vitro effects of simulated gastric juice on swallowed metal objects" (PubMed), Africa Check
